research_questions.statement: What are the properties and advantages of the graph attention mechanism?

provenance.text_excerpt: The recently published inductive method of Hamilton et al. (2017) samples a fixed-size neighborhood of each node, in order to keep its computational footprint consistent; this does not allow it access to the entirety of the neighborhood while performing inference. Moreover, this technique achieved some of its strongest results when an LSTM-based neighborhood aggregator is used. This assumes the existence of a consistent sequential node ordering across neighborhoods, and the authors have rectified it by consistently feeding randomly-ordered sequences to the LSTM. Our technique does not suffer from either of these issues—it works with the entirety of the neighborhood (at the expense of a variable computational footprint, which is still on-par with methods like the GCN), and does not assume any ordering within it.

claims.statement: GAT works with the entirety of the neighborhood and does not assume node ordering, unlike GraphSAGE's LSTM aggregator.

provenance.text_excerpt: Computationally, it is highly efficient: the operation of the self-attentional layer can be parallelized across all edges, and the computation of output features can be parallelized across all nodes. No eigendecompositions or similar computationally intensive matrix operations are required.

claims.statement: GAT is computationally efficient, parallelizable, and does not require eigendecompositions.

provenance.text_excerpt: The attention mechanism is applied in a shared manner to all edges in the graph, and therefore it does not depend on upfront access to the global graph structure or (features of) all of its nodes (a limitation of many prior techniques). This has several desirable implications: ... It makes our technique directly applicable to inductive learning

claims.statement: GAT does not depend on upfront access to global graph structure, making it applicable to inductive learning.

provenance.text_excerpt: As opposed to GCNs, our model allows for (implicitly) assigning different importances to nodes of a same neighborhood, enabling a leap in model capacity.

claims.statement: GAT allows assigning different importances to nodes in the same neighborhood, increasing model capacity.
